claims.text: Formation of a single-phase noble metal–based HEA nanoparticle is governed by the balance between rapid kinetic quenching and constituent-dependent surface and interfacial energies.
Rapid cooling kinetically traps atoms in a metastable high-entropy solid solution.
A marginally slower cooling rate permits enthalpic interactions to drive phase separation and elemental segregation.
Ultrafast heating and cooling can produce metastable, near-equiatomic, single-phase noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles.
Cooling rate should be varied systematically while composition is held constant.
Changing plasma-gas properties can alter the thermal history of HEA nanoparticles.
Controlled pulsed annealing can alter the local phase or elemental organization of HEA nanoparticles.
The applicable synthesis regime includes heating above 5000 K for less than 100 ms.
The hypothesis applies to compositions containing more than five near-equiatomic metals.
The hypothesis is applicable to nanoparticles smaller than roughly 50 nm.
Differences in constituent surface and interfacial energies mediate atomic mobility during cooling.
Limited atomic diffusion during rapid quenching preserves a single-phase, randomly mixed solid solution despite enthalpic preferences for segregation.
Reduced cooling rate gives atoms sufficient opportunity to reorganize into separated phases or elemental clusters.
Faster cooling will retain the near-equiatomic single-phase structure relative to the rapid-quench baseline.
Slower cooling will produce detectable phase separation, elemental segregation, and changes in particle morphology.
Differences in melting point, vapor pressure, and oxidation kinetics may also affect phase stability during cooling.
A lack of significant differences in phase purity, elemental distribution, and morphology between slower-cooled and rapidly quenched samples would falsify the proposed cooling-rate mechanism.
